messages.subject: Perception bias
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a very brief question regarding perception bias.

Perception bias occurs when observers miss visible animals because of environmental conditions, fatigue, etc.

However, I was wondering if distance itself would also be classed as a factor leading to perception bias?

Thank you in advance.
Regards,

Melissa

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Perception bias
messages.body_plain:
Hi Melissa,

I don't think distance, in and of itself, can be classed as a perception bias in distance analysis because the effect of distance on detectability is explicitly what distance analysis is supposed to account for. Bias can refer to any factor that tends to result in a (systematic) divergence between the conclusions of a study and the truth. So any factor whose effect on the variable under study is adequately accounted for in an analysis cannot (I think!) be considered a bias.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects
messages.body_plain:
Honnavalli

Methods for using line transect sampling with transects that curve has been examined in a 2001 publication by Hiby and Krishna

Hiby, L. and Krishna, M.B. (2001), Line transect sampling from a curving path. Biometrics, 57: 727-731. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00727.x <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00727.x>

In short, if the paths are curved, as opposed to wiggly, standard analysis methods could be used with shortest distance between the animal and the path used as the "perpendicular" distance measure.  The challenge in the field is to measure this distance accurately.

messages.subject: Density estimates from dsm?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Sorry if this is a stupid question but is it possible to obtain density estimates from a dsm? I've used dsms to estimate the abundance per grid cell and the overall abundance for my study site (2001 individuals). Is it only possible to obtain reliable density estimates through distance sampling? Or could I do a simple calculation to obtain mean density (individuals/km2), eg. divide the total estimated abundance given by dsm by the size of the study site in km?

I'm confused because most of the papers I am reading that have used dsm give estimates for abundance, but a few give additional estimates for density with no clear indication of how they calculated them- perhaps they just obtained them through distance sampling.

Thanks for your help,

Grace

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] setting intervals in data filter or diagnostics when working with radial distances
messages.body_plain:
Urvi

I'm assuming your question relates to analysis of point transect data, where radial distances are recorded and that's how I will answer.  Line transect data can also be collected using radial distance and bearing, but I'll not address that.

There is no need to bin data by setting cutpoints for binning data with point transect data.  Using exact distance measures will work just fine.  When creating bins for fitting detection functions, the shape of the detection function will depend upon the choice of cutpoints used for binning.  Cutpoint choice is largely subjective. Under normal circumstances, you would avoid subjective decisions in analysis, as subjectivity lessens the likelihood that analyses are repeatable.

Eric Rexstad

Grace

I assume you are using the R package `dsm`.  The `dsm` function in that package can produce cell-specific estimates of either abundance or density, depending upon what the user specifies on the right-hand side of the `formula` argument to the `dsm` function.

Have a close read of the `Details` section of the help for the `dsm` function.  Hopefully that will resolve your questions.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to estimate the density on curved/undulating transects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kumara and list,

I expect you know this, but in case not: one thing to bear in mind since
you are planning to use paths is that if you do not follow random
transects (e.g., systematic random) placed within your study area then
there are two issues with using the data to estimate density.

First, macaque density in the vicinity of the paths may not be
representative of that through your study area of interest.  For
example, paths tend to be on shallower ground but macaques may prefer
steeper ground.  Also, macaques may be repelled from paths if they don't
like being close to humans.  There are many other reasons why sampling
paths may not be the same as sampling random habitat, from the macaque
density point of view.

Second, if there is any kind of macaque density gradient going away from
the path (e.g., macaques may avoid being directly on paths, or the
opposite, they may like to use paths) then you cannot interpret the
pattern of detected distances as being about detectability, so you
cannot reliably estimate the detection function.

The first issue can be addressed to some extent by using the data
collected to build a model of factors affecting density (so called
"density surface modelling") but this is requires a good level of
training, and also if the transects completely avoid some habitats then
a reliable model is not possible.  There are methods to deal with the
second issue also, which involve doing the survey in a slightly
different way (doing a series of points along the track and collecting
the angle to detected animals - this will only work if the density
change around the track is very local).

I appreciate that it may be impossible to survey anywhere other than
tracks.  But I encourage you to consider the above issues and how much
of a problem they could potentially cause you.  Perhaps for macaques
neither of these issues are big enough to affect inference unduly.

I'd be happy to discuss this further off the list if that would be helpful.

Best wishes, Len Thomas

--

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] designing survey
messages.body_plain:
Banya

I'll not create a video regarding data entry for recce surveys at the moment.  It is actually a complicated analysis requiring two passes through the data.

The first pass uses data from recce effort (stratum label "recce") as well as planned survey effort (stratum label "planned") to compute encounter rate and variability in encounter rates.  The second pass uses only detections from the planned survey effort (accomplished via a data filter on stratum type) to fit a detection function.  The secret to performing the multi-pass analysis is using stratum labels to identify the types of survey effort so the data filter can operate.  If you consult the paper by Walsh and White (1999), they suggest the detections made by recce effort might need to be calibrated with planned effort because observer rate of travel on recce effort might be much greater than on planned transects.
Walsh, P. D., and L. J. T. White. 1999. What it will take to monitor forest elephant populations. Conservation Biology 13:1194–1202.

The results of the two passes are then combined (along with their measures of precision) to produce density estimates.  Encounter rate (and its precision) coming from analysis pass 1 (using both types of effort) along with detection function parameter estimates (f_0 and precision) from analysis pass 2.  Uncertainty is propagated using the delta method (squared CV of density is sum of squared CVs of encounter rate, f_0 and group size).

Perhaps we could correspond off-list about your data organisation; feel free to write to my personal email address.  You could then report a summary of what we discussed back to the list.

Regarding the use of the survey design engine, I recommend you view the lectures and exercises on survey design found in Chapter 4 of our online distance sampling training:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/
